lessonTopics.title: Steroid-Sensitive Nephrotic Syndrome: First Episode, Relapses and Steroid-Sparing Agents

mustKnow.fact: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria (> 40 mg/m²/hr or urine protein-to-creatinine ratio > 2.0 mg/mg or 3+ on dipstick), hypoalbuminemia (< 2.5 g/dL), and generalized edema.
Initial therapy for first episode of SSNS is oral prednisolone at 60 mg/m²/day (or 2 mg/kg/day, maximum 60 mg) daily for 4-6 weeks, followed by 40 mg/m² (1.5 mg/kg) on alternate days for 4-6 weeks.

Complete remission is defined as dipstick trace or zero protein (or UPCR < 0.2 mg/mg) for 3 consecutive days; relapse is defined as dipstick >= 3+ protein (or UPCR > 2.0 mg/mg) for 3 consecutive days.

Frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome (FRNS) is >= 2 relapses within 6 months of initial response or >= 4 relapses in any 12-month period; steroid dependence (SDNS) is 2 consecutive relapses during steroid taper or within 14 days of cessation.

First-line steroid-sparing therapies include oral levamisole (2.5 mg/kg alternate days), cyclophosphamide (2 mg/kg/day for 8-12 weeks, cumulative limit 168-200 mg/kg), and mycophenolate mofetil (MMF 1200 mg/m²/day).
Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, 375 mg/m² IV 1-2 doses) targets B-cell depletion (CD19 < 1%) and maintains long-term remission in refractory steroid-dependent nephrotic syndrome.

Severe hypoalbuminemia (serum albumin < 2.0 g/dL), elevated fibrinogen, and urinary loss of antithrombin III create high thromboembolic risk, warranting avoidance of femoral venipuncture and prompt hydration.

Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis in nephrotic ascites is predominantly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae and E. coli, requiring pneumococcal conjugate vaccination and immediate empiric cefotaxime or ceftriaxone.

lessonTopics.title: Steroid-Resistant Nephrotic Syndrome: Genetics, CNI Therapy and Transplant Recurrence

mustKnow.fact: Steroid resistance (SRNS) is failure to achieve complete remission after 4-6 weeks of daily oral prednisolone at 60 mg/m²/day; late resistance occurs in children who previously responded.

Renal biopsy is indicated before treatment in children presenting < 1 year or > 12 years of age, macroscopic hematuria, persistent hypertension, low C3 complement, renal failure, or documented steroid resistance.
Up to 30% of pediatric SRNS is monogenic, caused by podocyte and slit diaphragm gene mutations: NPHS1 (nephrin), NPHS2 (podocin), WT1 (Denys-Drash / Frasier), PLCE1, LAMB2, and INF2.
Children with confirmed monogenic genetic podocytopathies do not respond to immunosuppressive therapy; steroids and calcineurin inhibitors should be rapidly tapered to avoid toxicity.

In non-genetic SRNS, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus 0.1-0.15 mg/kg/day targeting trough 5-8 ng/mL, or cyclosporine targeting trough 100-150 ng/mL) induce complete or partial remission in 70-80% of patients.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis is classified into 5 variants: tip (best prognosis, steroid responsive), cellular, perihilar, collapsing (worst prognosis, rapid progression to ESRD), and not-otherwise-specified (NOS).

mustKnow.term: Circulating permeability factor and recurrence post-transplant
mustKnow.fact: Idiopathic non-genetic FSGS recurs in 30-50% of renal allografts within 48 hours post-transplant due to circulating permeability factor (suPAR / anti-UCHL1), treated with urgent plasma exchange and rituximab.
ACE inhibitors (enalapril) or ARBs (losartan) reduce intraglomerular capillary pressure and proteinuria by 30-50% in SRNS, while monitoring for hyperkalemia and acute drops in eGFR.

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Nephrotic Syndrome: Finnish Type, Denys-Drash and Early Management

mustKnow.term: Timing definition of congenital and infantile NS
mustKnow.fact: Congenital nephrotic syndrome (CNS) presents within the first 3 months of life (0-90 days); infantile nephrotic syndrome presents between 3 and 12 months of life.

Finnish type CNS is an autosomal recessive mutation in NPHS1 (19q13.1) encoding nephrin, presenting with massive intrauterine proteinuria, elevated maternal alpha-fetoprotein (AFP > 10 MoM), and enlarged placenta (> 25% infant birth weight).

mustKnow.term: NPHS2 podocin mutations and age of onset
mustKnow.fact: NPHS2 mutations (1q25-q31) encoding podocin cause autosomal recessive steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome presenting from early infancy up to adolescence, refractory to steroids.

mustKnow.term: Denys-Drash syndrome triad and WT1 mutations
mustKnow.fact: Denys-Drash syndrome is caused by missense WT1 mutations (11p13 exon 8/9), featuring triad of early-onset diffuse mesangial sclerosis (DMS), 46,XY disorder of sex development, and > 90% risk of Wilms tumor.

mustKnow.term: Frasier syndrome WT1 donor splice site
mustKnow.fact: Frasier syndrome results from WT1 intron 9 splice-site mutations, presenting with adolescent FSGS, 46,XY female sex reversal, streak gonads, and high risk of gonadoblastoma.

Management of Finnish CNS requires daily IV 20% albumin infusions (3-4 g/kg/day), ACE inhibitors, indomethacin to reduce GFR and urinary protein loss, and thyroxine repletion due to urinary thyroglobulin loss.
Bilateral nephrectomy with peritoneal dialysis is performed when the infant reaches 7-9 kg weight to halt life-threatening protein loss and prepare for renal transplantation at 10-12 kg.

Non-genetic congenital nephrotic syndrome can be caused by congenital syphilis, cytomegalovirus (CMV), toxoplasmosis, and congenital rubella, where proteinuria resolves upon antimicrobial eradication.

lessonTopics.title: Acute Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis: APSGN Latency, Complement and Course

mustKnow.fact: APSGN is triggered by Group A Streptococcus (speB and NAPlr antigens) after a latent period of 1-2 weeks following pharyngitis or 3-6 weeks following streptococcal pyoderma (impetigo).
Clinical presentation features the nephritic triad: gross hematuria (tea-colored or cola-colored smoky urine), edema (periorbital and pretibial), and hypertension with oliguria.

Serum complement C3 and CH50 are depressed in > 90% of APSGN cases via alternative complement activation, and must normalize within 6-8 weeks; persistence beyond 8 weeks mandates renal biopsy for MPGN/C3G.
Elevated or rising anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titer is positive in 80% following pharyngitis, whereas anti-DNase B is superior (> 90% positive) for post-pyoderma impetigo nephritis.

mustKnow.term: Light and electron microscopy subepithelial humps
mustKnow.fact: Renal biopsy reveals diffuse endocapillary proliferative GN with neutrophil infiltration; electron microscopy classically demonstrates discrete dome-shaped subepithelial electron-dense humps.
Immunofluorescence demonstrates coarse granular deposition of C3 and IgG along the glomerular capillary loops and mesangium, described as starry sky or garland appearance.
Management of hypertensive emergencies in APSGN requires fluid and sodium restriction, intravenous furosemide (1-2 mg/kg), and calcium channel blockers (amlodipine, nicardipine, or labetalol).
Diuresis ensues in 1-2 weeks; gross hematuria resolves in 2-4 weeks; hypertension normalizes in 2-3 weeks; microhematuria may persist harmlessly for up to 1-2 years.

lessonTopics.title: IgA Nephropathy and IgA Vasculitis HSP Nephritis: Oxford Classification and Care

mustKnow.fact: IgA nephropathy typically presents with recurrent episodes of gross macroscopic hematuria developing concurrently (within 24-48 hours) with an upper respiratory tract infection (synpharyngitic hematuria).

Pathogenesis involves elevated circulatory galactose-deficient IgA1 (Hit 1), anti-glycan autoantibodies (Hit 2), immune complex formation (Hit 3), and mesangial deposition triggering inflammation (Hit 4).

The revised Oxford classification scores M (mesangial hypercellularity > 50%), E (endocapillary hypercellularity), S (segmental glomerulosclerosis), T (tubular atrophy / interstitial fibrosis > 25%), and C (crescents > 0%).
For persistent proteinuria > 0.5-1.0 g/day/1.73m², maximum tolerated ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy is recommended for at least 90 days prior to considering immunosuppression.
Targeted-release oral budesonide (16 mg daily designed to deliver drug to distal ileum Peyer patches) significantly reduces proteinuria and slows eGFR loss in high-risk IgA nephropathy.

IgA vasculitis presents with the classic tetrad of non-thrombocytopenic palpable purpura (dependent lower limbs/buttocks), arthralgia/arthritis, colicky abdominal pain (intussusception risk), and glomerulonephritis.

Renal biopsy showing crescents in > 50% of glomeruli in IgA vasculitis nephritis warrants aggressive therapy with intravenous pulsed methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/dose, max 1000 mg) and cyclophosphamide.

All children diagnosed with IgA vasculitis require serial blood pressure and urinalysis screening weekly for the first month, then every 2-4 weeks for at least 6 months to detect late-onset nephritis.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Lupus Nephritis: ISN/RPS Classes, Induction and Targeted Therapies

mustKnow.fact: Renal involvement occurs in 50-80% of children with systemic lupus erythematosus, carrying greater severity and requiring more aggressive therapy than adult-onset SLE.

Classification comprises Class I (minimal mesangial), Class II (mesangial proliferative), Class III (focal proliferative < 50% glomeruli), Class IV (diffuse proliferative >= 50%), Class V (membranous), and Class VI (advanced sclerosing >= 90%).

Induction for proliferative lupus nephritis consists of high-dose corticosteroids plus either mycophenolate mofetil (1200 mg/m²/day) or intravenous pulsed cyclophosphamide (Euro-Lupus or NIH low-dose regimen).
Belimumab (anti-BAFF/BLyS monoclonal antibody) is approved for active lupus nephritis in children >= 5 years, improving renal response rates and reducing corticosteroid exposure.
Diagnostic renal immunofluorescence in lupus nephritis reveals intense granular full house staining positive for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, and C1q along capillary walls and mesangium.
Active proliferative lupus flares correlate tightly with rising anti-dsDNA antibody titers and consumption of serum complement C3 and C4.
All pediatric lupus nephritis patients should receive hydroxychloroquine (3-5 mg/kg/day, max 200-400 mg) unless contraindicated, reducing flares, thrombotic events, and renal damage.
Maintenance therapy with oral mycophenolate mofetil (or azathioprine) combined with low-dose prednisone must be sustained for at least 3-5 years before contemplating gradual withdrawal.

lessonTopics.title: Alport Syndrome and Thin Basement Membrane Disease: Type IV Collagen Genetics

mustKnow.fact: X-linked Alport syndrome accounts for 85% of cases and is caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A5 on chromosome Xq22.3 encoding the alpha-5 chain of type IV collagen.
Autosomal recessive Alport syndrome (15% of cases) results from homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 (chromosome 2q36.3), causing early ESRD in both sexes equally.
Diagnostic electron microscopy reveals irregular thickening, thinning, and characteristic splitting/lamellation of the glomerular basement membrane lamina densa (basket-weave pattern).
High-frequency bilateral sensorineural hearing loss emerges during late childhood or early adolescence (never present in neonates) in up to 80-90% of affected males with X-linked Alport.
Anterior lenticonus (conical protrusion of the anterior lens capsule into the anterior chamber) and perimacular fleck retinopathy are pathognomonic ocular hallmarks of Alport syndrome.
Initiating ramipril or enalapril at early microalbuminuria stage delays onset of end-stage renal disease by decades compared to untreated historical cohorts.
Approximately 3-5% of transplanted male Alport patients develop de novo anti-GBM crescentic nephritis because their immune system recognizes normal allograft collagen IV alpha-5 chains as foreign.
Heterozygous mutations in COL4A3 or COL4A4 cause thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria), featuring diffuse uniform thinning of GBM (< 200-250 nm) with normal renal function.

lessonTopics.title: C3 Glomerulopathy and MPGN: Alternative Complement Dysregulation and Management

mustKnow.fact: MPGN is modernly categorized by immunofluorescence into immune complex-mediated MPGN (Ig-positive with complement, driven by infections/autoimmunity) and complement-mediated C3 glomerulopathy (C3-dominant with absent/scant Igs).

mustKnow.term: C3 glomerulonephritis vs Dense Deposit Disease (DDD)
mustKnow.fact: C3G is subdivided on electron microscopy into Dense Deposit Disease (extremely osmophilic, ribbon-like serpentine electron-dense intramembranous deposits) and C3GN (mesangial and subendothelial/subepithelial deposits).
C3NeF is an IgG autoantibody that stabilizes the alternative pathway C3 convertase (C3bBb), extending its half-life and causing relentless fluid-phase C3 consumption and profound hypocomplementemia.

Dense deposit disease is strongly associated with acquired partial lipodystrophy (Barraquer-Simons syndrome, progressive loss of subcutaneous fat from head down) and ocular drusen of the retinal pigment epithelium.
Both MPGN and C3G show lobular glomerular accentuation, endocapillary proliferation, and mesangial interposition splitting the capillary basement membrane into a double contour (tram-track sign).
Evaluation requires testing for CFH, CFI, CD46 (MCP), CFHR1-5 hybrid genes, anti-factor H autoantibodies, and alternative pathway components (Bb, sC5b-9).
First-line immunosuppressive therapy for progressive proteinuria in C3G consists of mycophenolate mofetil (1200 mg/m²/day) plus oral glucocorticoids, achieving stabilization in 50% of patients.

mustKnow.term: Pegcetacoplan and Factor B inhibitor therapies
mustKnow.fact: Novel proximal complement inhibitors targeting C3 (pegcetacoplan) or Factor B (iptacopan) demonstrate significant reduction in glomerular C3 deposition and proteinuria in clinical trials.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric AKI: KDIGO & pRIFLE Staging, Biomarkers and Fluid Overload

mustKnow.fact: KDIGO defines AKI Stage 1 as serum creatinine increase >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48h or 1.5-1.9x baseline; Stage 2 as 2.0-2.9x baseline; Stage 3 as >= 3.0x baseline or SCr >= 4.0 mg/dL or initiation of RRT or eGFR < 35 mL/min/1.73m² in children < 18 years.
Oliguria staging requires: Stage 1 (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6-12 hours), Stage 2 (< 0.5 mL/kg/hr for >= 12 hours), and Stage 3 (< 0.3 mL/kg/hr for >= 24 hours or anuria for >= 12 hours).

Percent fluid overload (%FO) is calculated as [(Fluid In - Fluid Out) / Admission Weight] x 100%; fluid overload > 10-15% in critically ill children is independently associated with a 3-fold increase in mortality.

Urinary and serum Neutrophil Gelatinase-Associated Lipocalin (NGAL > 150 ng/mL) and Kidney Injury Molecule-1 (KIM-1) rise within 2-4 hours of ischemic/toxic insult, preceding serum creatinine rise by 24-48 hours.

FST evaluates tubular integrity by administering IV furosemide (1.0 mg/kg in loop-diuretic naive, 1.5 mg/kg if previously exposed); urine output < 2 mL/kg over 2 hours predicts progression to severe AKI.

The pediatric Renal Angina Index multiplies risk factors (ICU admission, solid organ transplant) by injury score (creatinine rise or fluid overload); RAI >= 8 identifies patients needing biomarker testing.
FeNa = [(Urine Na x Serum Cr) / (Serum Na x Urine Cr)] x 100%; FeNa < 1% (< 2.5% in neonates) suggests prerenal azotemia, while FeNa > 2% indicates intrinsic acute tubular necrosis (ATN).
The NINJA initiative showed that systematic screening for exposure to >= 3 nephrotoxins simultaneously or >= 3 days of aminoglycosides reduces hospital-acquired AKI rates by 38%.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Renal Replacement Therapy: CRRT, Peritoneal Dialysis and Hemodialysis

mustKnow.term: Absolute indications for acute pediatric RRT
mustKnow.fact: Indications for acute RRT include refractory hyperkalemia (K > 6.5-7.0 mEq/L with ECG changes), refractory metabolic acidosis (pH < 7.15), symptomatic uremia (encephalopathy, pericarditis), and fluid overload > 10-15%.

mustKnow.term: Peritoneal dialysis catheter insertion and fill volume
mustKnow.fact: Acute PD is preferred in neonates and hemodynamically unstable infants; initial dwell volume starts at 10-20 mL/kg with gradual escalation to 30-40 mL/kg as tolerated without respiratory compromise.

mustKnow.term: CRRT modality selection (CVVH vs CVVHD vs CVVHDF)
mustKnow.fact: Continuous Veno-Venous Hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) combines convective solute removal of middle/large molecules with diffusive clearance of small molecules, ideal for sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction.

mustKnow.term: Vascular access sizing in pediatric CRRT
mustKnow.fact: Double-lumen catheter sizes depend on patient weight: 6.5 Fr for neonates (< 3 kg), 7-8 Fr for infants (3-10 kg), 8-9 Fr for children (10-30 kg), and 11-13.5 Fr for adolescents (> 30 kg).

RCA is superior to systemic heparin for pediatric CRRT filter survival; pre-filter citrate binds calcium, while IV calcium chloride is infused systemically to maintain patient ionized calcium between 1.1-1.3 mmol/L.

Citrate accumulation manifests as high anion-gap metabolic acidosis and total-to-ionized calcium ratio > 2.5 (Ca_tot / Ca_ion), requiring reduction of citrate infusion or temporary switch to saline flushes.

Dedicated miniature platforms (CARPEDIEM and NIDUS) reduce extracorporeal circuit volume to < 10-15 mL (< 10% of neonate blood volume), eliminating the need for blood priming in low birth weight infants.

mustKnow.term: Target effluent dose in pediatric CRRT
mustKnow.fact: The recommended delivered effluent clearance dose in pediatric CRRT is 20-25 mL/kg/hr; higher doses do not improve survival and exacerbate electrolyte and micronutrient depletion.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric CKD: Etiology, Schwartz Formula, Staging and Progression Retardation

mustKnow.term: Pediatric CKD etiology vs adult CKD
mustKnow.fact: Unlike adults where diabetes and hypertension dominate, pediatric CKD is primarily caused by congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT, 50%) and hereditary nephropathies (20%).

mustKnow.term: Bedside Schwartz formula for pediatric eGFR
mustKnow.fact: Bedside Schwartz equation is: eGFR (mL/min/1.73m²) = 0.413 x Height (cm) / Serum Creatinine (mg/dL), validated for children aged 1 to 16 years.
CKD is staged by GFR: Stage 1 (>= 90 with kidney damage), Stage 2 (60-89), Stage 3a (45-59), Stage 3b (30-44), Stage 4 (15-29, severe reduction), and Stage 5 (< 15 mL/min/1.73m², kidney failure).

mustKnow.term: Blood pressure target to retard progression
mustKnow.fact: The ESCAPE trial established that strict ambulatory blood pressure control to < 50th percentile using ACE inhibitors significantly slows CKD progression and reduces risk of ESRD by 35%.

mustKnow.term: Growth failure and recombinant human GH
mustKnow.fact: Persistent height velocity < 25th percentile or height SDS < -2.0 despite optimal nutrition and metabolic acidosis correction warrants recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH 0.045-0.05 mg/kg/day).
Serum bicarbonate must be maintained >= 22 mEq/L using oral sodium bicarbonate (1-3 mEq/kg/day) to prevent bone mineral dissolution, muscle wasting, and accelerated CKD decline.
SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) reduce intraglomerular hyperfiltration and albuminuria in adolescents with proteinuric CKD, expanding from adult nephroprotection trials.

Pre-emptive living donor kidney transplantation (before starting maintenance dialysis) is the gold standard for pediatric CKD stage 5 (eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73m²), maximizing neurocognitive and linear growth outcomes.

lessonTopics.title: CKD-Mineral and Bone Disorder: Phosphate Binders, Vitamin D and FGF-23 Axis

mustKnow.fact: Declining GFR causes phosphate retention, triggering osteocyte secretion of FGF-23 and downregulating renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase (CYP27B1), leading to 1,25(OH)2D deficiency, hypocalcemia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism.

KDIGO recommends maintaining intact PTH at 1.5-3x upper normal limit in CKD Stage 4 (70-150 pg/mL) and 2-9x upper normal limit in CKD Stage 5 / dialysis (150-300 pg/mL) to avoid adynamic bone disease.

Calcium-based binders (calcium carbonate, calcium acetate) are taken with meals; non-calcium binders (sevelamer carbonate 50-100 mg/kg/day) are preferred if hypercalcemia or vascular calcification develops.
Active vitamin D sterols (calcitriol 0.25-1 mcg/day or alfacalcidol) suppress parathyroid PTH gene expression; therapy must be paused if serum calcium x phosphate product exceeds 55-65 mg²/dL².

Cinacalcet (oral allosteric modulator of calcium-sensing receptor) or etelcalcetide is utilized in adolescents on hemodialysis with severe secondary hyperparathyroidism refractory to active vitamin D.

Over-suppression of PTH (intact PTH < 100 pg/mL) leads to adynamic bone disease characterized by absent bone turnover, osteomalacia, inability to buffer calcium, and severe metastatic arterial calcification.
Renal osteodystrophy in pediatric patients uniquely produces slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), genu valgum (knock-knees), metaphyseal cupping, and rachitic rosary.
Dietary phosphate restriction to 100% of Dietary Reference Intake (DRI) for age is initiated as soon as PTH rises above normal, avoiding processed foods rich in inorganic phosphate additives.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Anemia of CKD: Iron Repletion, ESA Targets and Resistance

mustKnow.fact: Anemia of CKD is primarily driven by peritubular interstitial cell erythropoietin deficiency, compounded by hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration, shortened erythrocyte survival, and chronic inflammation.

mustKnow.term: Target hemoglobin range in pediatric CKD
mustKnow.fact: KDIGO recommends targeting hemoglobin between 10.0 and 12.0 g/dL; targeting normal hemoglobin (> 13 g/dL) is strictly avoided due to increased risks of hypertension, stroke, and vascular thrombosis.

mustKnow.term: Iron repletion thresholds prior to ESA
mustKnow.fact: Iron status must be optimized before starting ESA therapy: target transferrin saturation (TSAT) > 20% and serum ferritin > 100 ng/mL in non-dialysis CKD (> 200 ng/mL in hemodialysis).
Epoetin alfa is started at 50-100 U/kg/dose subcutaneously or IV 1-3 times weekly, or darbepoetin alfa at 0.45 mcg/kg once weekly or every 2 weeks.

For hemodialysis patients or severe oral iron intolerance, IV iron sucrose (1-2 mg/kg per dose, max 100 mg) is administered weekly up to a cumulative replacement dose calculated by the Ganzoni equation.

ESA hyporesponsiveness is failure to achieve target Hb despite high ESA doses (> 300 U/kg/week epoetin); primary causes are absolute iron deficiency, occult infection, hyperparathyroidism, and aluminum toxicity.

Development of sudden refractory anemia with reticulocytopenia (< 10,000/mm³) after ESA treatment suggests anti-erythropoietin neutralizing antibodies, requiring immediate ESA cessation and bone marrow biopsy.
Hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase (HIF-PH) inhibitors promote endogenous erythropoietin transcription and improve iron bioavailability, under pediatric clinical trial evaluation.

lessonTopics.title: STEC D+ Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome: Shiga Toxin, Microangiopathy and Supportive Care

mustKnow.fact: Hemolytic uremic syndrome is defined by the clinical triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (Coombs-negative, schistocytes), thrombocytopenia (< 150,000/mm³), and acute kidney injury.

mustKnow.term: Shiga toxin pathogenesis and Gb3 receptors
mustKnow.fact: Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7, O26, O104) produces Shiga toxin (Stx1 and Stx2), which binds globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) receptors on glomerular endothelial cells, halting protein synthesis and causing microvascular thrombosis.

Antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole) and antimotility agents (loperamide) administered during the prodromal diarrheal phase increase Shiga toxin release and elevate risk of HUS by up to 17-fold.
Early intravenous volume expansion with isotonic saline (10-15 mL/kg/hr initially) during the diarrheal prodrome preserves renal microvascular perfusion and halves the requirement for acute dialysis.

Platelet transfusions are strictly contraindicated in HUS because transfused platelets fuel microvascular thrombosis, and are reserved exclusively for life-threatening intracranial or active surgical hemorrhage.
mustKnow.source: British Committee for Standards in Haematology

mustKnow.term: Stx stool PCR and sorbitol-MacConkey agar
mustKnow.fact: Diagnosis is confirmed by stool culture on Sorbitol-MacConkey agar (O157 strains are sorbitol non-fermenting, appearing colorless) or enzyme immunoassay / PCR for Stx1 and Stx2 genes.

mustKnow.term: Indications for acute dialysis in D+ HUS
mustKnow.fact: Acute peritoneal dialysis or hemodialysis is required in over 50% of children with D+ HUS due to anuria, severe fluid overload, symptomatic uremia, or intractable hyperkalemia.

Up to 30% of children surviving D+ HUS develop hypertension, proteinuria, or chronic kidney disease years later due to hyperfiltration in surviving nephrons, necessitating annual BP and UPCR follow-up.

lessonTopics.title: Atypical HUS: Alternative Complement Gene Variants and Terminal C5 Inhibition

mustKnow.fact: Atypical HUS (aHUS) represents uncontrolled alternative complement activation on endothelial surfaces, driven by loss-of-function mutations in regulatory proteins (CFH, CFI, CD46/MCP) or gain-of-function mutations in C3 and CFB.
Mutations in CFH (chromosome 1q31.3) account for 25-30% of aHUS cases, carrying a 70% risk of progressing to end-stage renal disease or death within one year if untreated.

mustKnow.term: Anti-factor H autoantibody HUS and CFHR1-3 deletion
mustKnow.fact: Anti-CFH autoantibodies cause 10-15% of pediatric aHUS (predominant in India), strongly linked to homozygous deletion of CFHR1-CFHR3, requiring plasma exchange plus corticosteroids and rituximab.
Eculizumab (recombinant humanized anti-C5 monoclonal antibody) halts terminal membrane attack complex (C5b-9) assembly, inducing hematologic remission and renal recovery in > 80% of aHUS patients.

Terminal complement blockade increases susceptibility to Neisseria meningitidis by 2000-fold; mandatory meningococcal vaccination (MenACWY and MenB) and daily oral prophylactic penicillin/erythromycin must be initiated.
mustKnow.source: CDC Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices

mustKnow.fact: Ravulizumab is an engineered long-acting C5 inhibitor with extended terminal half-life requiring IV maintenance infusions only once every 8 weeks in children >= 20 kg (every 4 weeks if < 20 kg).
Isolated membrane cofactor protein (CD46/MCP) mutations carry a low risk of post-transplant recurrence (< 20%) because the normal donor kidney expresses wild-type CD46 on graft endothelium.

Mutations in diacylglycerol kinase epsilon (DGKE) cause an infantile recessively inherited TMA without complement activation, manifesting before age 1 with relapsing nephrotic-range proteinuria and microangiopathy refractory to eculizumab.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric TTP: Congenital Upshaw-Schulman Syndrome vs Immune ADAMTS13 Deficiency

mustKnow.fact: TTP is defined pathologically by severe deficiency of the von Willebrand factor cleaving protease ADAMTS13 activity to < 10% of normal, leading to ultra-large vWF multimer accumulation.

Congenital TTP (Upshaw-Schulman syndrome) is an autosomal recessive mutation in ADAMTS13 (9q34.2), presenting in neonates with severe Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia, hyperbilirubinemia, and thrombocytopenia.

The PLASMIC score stratifies probability of severe ADAMTS13 deficiency based on platelets < 30k, hemolysis, no active cancer, no transplant, MCV < 90, INR < 1.5, and creatinine < 2.0 mg/dL; score 6-7 indicates high probability.

Acquired immune TTP requires immediate daily therapeutic plasma exchange (1.0-1.5 plasma volumes, 40-60 mL/kg) with fresh frozen plasma replacement and systemic corticosteroids until platelet count normalizes (> 150k for 2 days).

Caplacizumab (bivalent anti-vWF nanobody targeting the A1 domain, 10 mg daily) blocks platelet adhesion to ultra-large vWF multimers, significantly accelerating platelet count recovery and reducing ischemic complications.

mustKnow.term: Prophylactic plasma infusions in congenital TTP
mustKnow.fact: Patients with congenital Upshaw-Schulman syndrome do not develop antibodies and are managed with regular prophylactic fresh frozen plasma infusions (10-15 mL/kg every 2-3 weeks).
Recombinant human ADAMTS13 (40 IU/kg IV) provides targeted enzyme replacement without the volume and allergic risks of plasma transfusion in congenital TTP.
In immune-mediated TTP, rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly for 4 doses) eliminates ADAMTS13 autoantibody-producing B-cell clones, substantially lowering the 1-year relapse rate from 40% to < 10%.

lessonTopics.title: Bartter vs Gitelman Syndromes: Loop vs DCT Transporters and Urinary Calcium

mustKnow.term: Metabolic alkalosis and blood pressure phenotype
mustKnow.fact: Both Bartter and Gitelman syndromes feature hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with normal or low blood pressure despite marked hyperreninemic hyperaldosteronism.

Bartter syndrome impairs thick ascending limb sodium chloride reabsorption: Type I (SLC12A1 / NKCC2), Type II (KCNJ1 / ROMK), Type III (CLCNKB / ClC-Kb), Type IV (BSND / Barttin with sensorineural deafness), and Type V (CASR gain-of-function).
Antenatal Bartter (Types I and II) presents with maternal polyhydramnios, extreme preterm delivery, life-threatening neonatal salt wasting, isosthenuria, and early nephrocalcinosis.

mustKnow.term: Gitelman syndrome SLC12A3 and NCCT defect
mustKnow.fact: Gitelman syndrome is an autosomal recessive mutation in SLC12A3 encoding the thiazide-sensitive NaCl cotransporter (NCCT) in the distal convoluted tubule, typically manifesting in school-age or adolescence.

Urinary calcium excretion cleanly differentiates the two: Bartter syndrome causes hypercalciuria (urine Ca/Cr ratio > 0.2 mg/mg) and nephrocalcinosis, whereas Gitelman syndrome causes hypocalciuria (urine Ca/Cr < 0.1 mg/mg).
Severe persistent hypomagnesemia (serum Mg < 1.7 mg/dL) due to down-regulation of TRPM6 channels in the DCT is a hallmark of Gitelman syndrome, leading to chondrocalcinosis and tetany.
High renal prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) drives polyuria in Bartter; cyclooxygenase inhibitors (indomethacin 1.5-3.0 mg/kg/day or celecoxib) close loop signaling, restoring GFR and electrolyte balance.
High-dose oral potassium chloride repletion is supplemented with potassium-sparing diuretics (spironolactone 2-4 mg/kg/day, amiloride, or eplerenone) to counteract secondary hyperaldosteronism.

lessonTopics.title: Renal Tubular Acidosis: Distal Type 1, Proximal Type 2, Fanconi and Type 4

mustKnow.term: Shared hallmark of normal anion gap acidosis
mustKnow.fact: All forms of renal tubular acidosis present with normal serum anion gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis: Anion Gap = Na - (Cl + HCO3) between 8 and 12 mEq/L.

Type 1 (distal) RTA is caused by failure of alpha-intercalated cells to excrete H+ ions (SLC4A1 / AE1, ATP6V1B1 / ATP6V0A4 with deafness), resulting in inability to acidify urine below pH 5.5 despite severe systemic acidemia.

mustKnow.term: Positive urine anion gap in distal RTA
mustKnow.fact: Urine Anion Gap [U_Na + U_K - U_Cl] is positive in distal RTA (indicating impaired urinary ammonium NH4+ excretion), whereas it is strongly negative in gastrointestinal bicarbonate loss (diarrhea).

Systemic acidosis enhances proximal tubular citrate reabsorption, causing severe hypocitraturia and hypercalciuria; alkaline urine precipitates calcium phosphate, leading to medullary nephrocalcinosis and rickets.

mustKnow.term: Proximal RTA Type 2 and Fanconi syndrome
mustKnow.fact: Type 2 (proximal) RTA reflects defective proximal bicarbonate threshold reabsorption (< 15-18 mEq/L) via SLC4A4 (NBCe1), frequently part of generalized Fanconi syndrome (cystinosis, Lowe syndrome, galactosemia, tyrosinemia).

mustKnow.term: Fractional excretion of bicarbonate in Type 2
mustKnow.fact: When serum bicarbonate is normalized to 24 mEq/L via IV bicarbonate infusion, proximal RTA shows fractional excretion of bicarbonate (FE_HCO3) > 15-20%, whereas in distal RTA it remains < 5%.

Infantile nephropathic cystinosis (CTNS gene encoding cystinosin) is the most common genetic cause of Fanconi syndrome; oral cysteamine (1.3 g/m²/day) and cysteamine eye drops deplete intralysosomal cystine crystals.

Type 4 RTA is characterized by hyperkalemia due to aldosterone deficiency or aldosterone resistance (PHA Type 1: SCNN1A/B/G or NR3C2), treated with fludrocortisone, dietary potassium restriction, and sodium polystyrene sulfonate.

lessonTopics.title: Congenital Nephrogenic Diabetes Insipidus: AVPR2, AQP2 and Pharmacotherapy

mustKnow.fact: Over 90% of congenital nephrogenic diabetes insipidus cases are X-linked recessive mutations in AVPR2 (Xq28) encoding the vasopressin V2 receptor on collecting duct principal cells.
Mutations in AQP2 (chromosome 12q13.12) encoding the apical aquaporin-2 water channel account for 10% of cases, inherited in autosomal recessive or dominant patterns.
Infants present in the first weeks of life with severe irritability, unexplained fevers, poor feeding, failure to thrive, and life-threatening hypernatremic dehydration (serum Na > 160-170 mEq/L).

Administration of 1-desamino-8-D-arginine vasopressin (DDAVP 1-2 mcg SC or IV) fails to increase urine osmolality above 300 mOsm/kg or decrease urine volume in nephrogenic DI, distinguishing it from central DI.

Unrestricted access to free water is life-saving; infants require enteral tube feeding with low-solute formula to keep daily osmotic load < 15 mOsm/kg and replace urine losses exceeding 5-10 L/m²/day.
Hydrochlorothiazide (2-4 mg/kg/day) induces mild volume contraction, triggering compensatory proximal tubular sodium and water reabsorption and reducing distal delivery to collecting ducts by 30-50%.

Combining hydrochlorothiazide with amiloride (0.3-0.5 mg/kg/day) prevents hypokalemia and blocks ENaC channels; adding indomethacin (1-2 mg/kg/day) inhibits medullary prostaglandins and further reduces urine output.
Massive chronic high-volume polyuria produces severe non-obstructive bilateral hydroureteronephrosis and a distended myogenic bladder (megacystis-megaureter complex) requiring timed double voiding.

lessonTopics.title: Autosomal Recessive Polycystic Kidney Disease: PKHD1, Fibrocystin and Portal Hypertension

mustKnow.fact: ARPKD is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in PKHD1 (6p12.3-p12.2) encoding fibrocystin/polyductin, localized to the primary cilium and basal body of renal collecting duct and biliary epithelia.

Severe antenatal presentation features massive bilateral nephromegaly, severe oligohydramnios, Potter facies (compressed flat nose, low-set ears), pulmonary hypoplasia, and a 30% neonatal mortality rate from respiratory failure.

Renal ultrasonography demonstrates massively enlarged, symmetric, highly echogenic kidneys with poor corticomedullary differentiation and radial acoustic shadowing from millions of microscopic dilated collecting ducts.

All patients with ARPKD have congenital hepatic fibrosis (ductal plate malformation); children who survive the neonatal renal period present in childhood with portal hypertension, hypersplenism, and esophageal varices.
Non-obstructive cystic dilatation of the intrahepatic bile ducts (Caroli disease) predisposes to recurrent ascending bacterial cholangitis requiring prophylactic co-trimoxazole or cephalosporins.

Over 80% of children with ARPKD develop severe hypertension in the first months of life due to intrarenal ischemia and hyper-reninemia, requiring aggressive multi-drug therapy with ACE inhibitors and ARBs.
Despite severe portal hypertension and massive splenomegaly, hepatic synthetic function (serum albumin, bilirubin, and prothrombin time / INR) remains completely normal in uncomplicated CHF.
Dual organ liver-kidney transplantation is indicated in patients reaching ESRD who have concomitant recurrent life-threatening cholangitis, intractable variceal bleeding, or severe hypersplenism.

lessonTopics.title: ADPKD in Children vs Nephronophthisis: Corticomedullary Cysts and Ciliopathy Overlap

mustKnow.fact: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease results from PKD1 (16p13.3, 85%, polycystin-1, ESRD median age 54) or PKD2 (4q21, 15%, polycystin-2, ESRD median age 74) mutations.
In children < 15 years with an affected first-degree relative, the presence of >= 1 renal cyst of any size in either kidney has a positive predictive value > 95% for ADPKD.
Tolvaptan (oral selective V2 antagonist) slows total kidney volume (TKV) expansion and eGFR decline by inhibiting intracellular cAMP, approved in adolescents with rapidly progressive ADPKD.

Nephronophthisis is an autosomal recessive ciliopathy and the most common monogenic cause of pediatric ESRD; NPHP1 deletions (2q13) account for 20-25% of juvenile cases, reaching ESRD at median age 13 years.

Ultrasonography reveals normal or small-sized kidneys with increased parenchymal echogenicity, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, and characteristic cysts localized exclusively to the corticomedullary junction.

mustKnow.term: Polyuria, polydipsia and anemia out of proportion
mustKnow.fact: Children present with impaired urinary concentrating ability (polyuria, polydipsia, enuresis), salt wasting, and normocytic anemia disproportionately severe for their level of early renal dysfunction.
Senior-Loken syndrome pairs nephronophthisis with tapetoretinal degeneration (retinitis pigmentosa or Leber congenital amaurosis), diagnosed by electroretinography.
Joubert syndrome associates NPHP with cerebellar vermis hypoplasia (molar tooth sign on axial brain MRI), neonatal episodic tachypnea/apnea, and developmental delay.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Hypertension: AAP 2017 Blood Pressure Percentiles, Staging and Therapy

mustKnow.fact: For children aged 1-13 years, BP is classified by age, sex, and height percentiles: Normal (< 90th percentile), Elevated (>= 90th to < 95th or 120/80 mmHg), Stage 1 (>= 95th to < 95th + 12 mmHg), and Stage 2 (>= 95th + 12 mmHg or >= 140/90 mmHg).
For adolescents >= 13 years, staging aligns directly with adult AHA/ACC cutoffs: Normal (< 120/< 80 mmHg), Elevated (120-129/< 80), Stage 1 (130-139/80-89), and Stage 2 (>= 140/>= 90 mmHg).

mustKnow.term: Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) gold standard
mustKnow.fact: ABPM is mandatory to confirm hypertension and identify white-coat hypertension (elevated clinic BP, normal ABPM) or masked hypertension (normal clinic BP, elevated wake/sleep ABPM > 95th percentile).
In children < 6 years of age, hypertension is almost universally secondary (> 85%), with renal parenchymal disease (CAKUT, GN) and renovascular coarctation accounting for the vast majority.

Echocardiography to screen for left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH, defined as LV mass index >= 38.6 g/m^2.7 for children or > 51 g/m^2.7 for adolescent boys) is indicated at diagnosis of persistent hypertension.

First-line monotherapy classes in children are ACE inhibitors (enalapril, lisinopril), ARBs (losartan), and calcium channel blockers (amlodipine 0.1-0.6 mg/kg/day); thiazide diuretics are added as step two.

Hypertensive emergency features severe Stage 2 BP (> 30 mmHg above 95th percentile) with acute end-organ damage (encephalopathy, seizures, heart failure, retinopathy), requiring continuous IV nicardipine or labetalol.

mustKnow.term: Rate of BP reduction in emergency
mustKnow.fact: To prevent ischemic cerebral infarction, BP should be lowered by no more than 25% of the planned reduction in the first 8 hours, and normalized gradually over the subsequent 24-48 hours.

lessonTopics.title: Renovascular Hypertension in Children: Fibromuscular Dysplasia, Takayasu and Angioplasty

mustKnow.fact: Renovascular hypertension accounts for 10-15% of all secondary pediatric hypertension, caused by fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD, 60-70%), Takayasu arteritis, neurofibromatosis type 1, or middle aortic syndrome.
Unlike adults where medial fibroplasia (string-of-beads) dominates, pediatric renal FMD frequently exhibits intimal fibroplasia or perimedial fibroplasia with tubular or ostial narrowing.

mustKnow.term: Catheter digital subtraction angiography gold standard
mustKnow.fact: Conventional catheter digital subtraction angiography (DSA) remains the definitive diagnostic gold standard in children, detecting distal branch and intrarenal stenosis missed by CTA or MRA.
Balloon angioplasty without stenting is the primary intervention for pediatric non-ostial FMD, achieving clinical cure or marked improvement in > 70-80% of children.

mustKnow.term: ACE inhibitor contraindication in bilateral stenosis
mustKnow.fact: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are strictly contraindicated in bilateral renal artery stenosis or solitary functioning kidney stenosis because they ablate efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, causing sudden precipitous decline in GFR.

Takayasu arteritis presents with asymmetric limb pulses, bruits, and elevated inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP); revascularization must be delayed until corticosteroid / biologic therapy induces complete disease quiescence.
A selective renal vein renin ratio (affected kidney to contralateral normal kidney) > 1.5 indicates significant hemodynamic lateralization predicting successful surgical or angioplasty cure.
Ex-vivo microvascular bench reconstruction with renal autotransplantation into the iliac fossa is indicated for complex intrarenal branch stenosis or when balloon angioplasty fails.

lessonTopics.title: CAKUT Spectrum: PUJO, Posterior Urethral Valves and Vesicoureteral Reflux

mustKnow.term: Antenatal hydronephrosis grading (AP renal pelvic diameter)
mustKnow.fact: Antenatal hydronephrosis on ultrasound is graded by anteroposterior renal pelvic diameter (APRPD): >= 4-7 mm in second trimester and >= 7-10 mm in third trimester warrants postnatal surveillance.
Initial postnatal renal ultrasound is performed at 48-72 hours of life to avoid false-negative underestimation due to transient neonatal physiological oliguria, unless PUV is suspected.

PUV occurs exclusively in males, caused by congenital obstructing folds of the verumontanum (Type 1 Young classification), displaying a thick-walled trabeculated bladder and dilated posterior urethra (keyhole sign) on ultrasound.

Immediate neonatal management of PUV requires transurethral bladder catheterization (5-8 Fr feeding tube) followed by cystoscopic primary valve ablation; vesicostomy is performed if the urethra is too small.
PUJO is the most common cause of significant pediatric hydronephrosis; confirmed by 99mTc-MAG3 renography demonstrating prolonged washout half-time (T1/2 > 20 minutes) after furosemide (1 mg/kg).
Surgical pyeloplasty is indicated for differential renal function < 40%, a fall of > 10% on serial scans, worsening hydronephrosis, or recurrent febrile urinary tract infections.

Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) grades vesicoureteral reflux from Grade I (reflux into non-dilated ureter) to Grade V (massive reflux, severe tortuosity, and complete loss of papillary impressions).
The RIVUR trial demonstrated that daily co-trimoxazole or nitrofurantoin prophylaxis in children with Grades II-IV VUR reduces recurrent febrile UTIs by 50% without altering renal scarring.

lessonTopics.title: Pediatric Nephrolithiasis: Cystinuria, Primary Hyperoxaluria and Citrate Management

mustKnow.fact: Unlike adults where diet and lifestyle predominate, over 75-80% of children with nephrolithiasis have an underlying identifiable metabolic abnormality, with idiopathic hypercalciuria being the most common (40-50%).
Metabolic workup defines hypercalciuria (> 4 mg/kg/day), hyperoxaluria (> 0.5 mmol/1.73m²/day), hypocitraturia (< 320 mg/1.73m²/day), and hyperuricosuria (> 10 mg/kg/day).

PH1 is an autosomal recessive deficiency of hepatic alanine:glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGXT, 2q37.3), presenting in infancy with nephrocalcinosis, recurrent calcium oxalate monohydrate stones, and systemic oxalosis.
Lumasiran (subcutaneous RNA interference targeting glycolate oxidase / HAO1) depletes glyoxylate production, drastically reducing urinary oxalate excretion by > 65% in pediatric PH1.
Cystinuria impairs the dibasic amino acid transporter (COLA: cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine), forming radiopaque hexagonal flat crystals in acidic urine (cyanide-nitroprusside test positive).

mustKnow.term: Urinary alkalinization and tiopronin in cystinuria
mustKnow.fact: Cystine stone dissolution requires vigorous hydration (> 3 L/m²/day), potassium citrate to achieve urine pH >= 7.5, and thiol chelation drugs (tiopronin or D-penicillamine) to convert cystine to soluble mixed disulfides.
Citrate is a potent natural inhibitor of calcium stone crystallization; potassium citrate (1-2 mEq/kg/day divided TID) alkalinizes urine and restores urinary citrate excretion.

mustKnow.term: Nephrocalcinosis in preterm infants on furosemide
mustKnow.fact: Chronic loop diuretic (furosemide) administration in premature neonates causes massive hypercalciuria and medullary nephrocalcinosis in up to 60%, reversible upon transitioning to chlorothiazide.
